834.title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
834.hook: the whole day becomes a race against the sun, and the sun seems to set too early
834.howItsDone: The day of Jayadratha's death is told in the Drona Parva, and retellings return to the false sunset and Krishna's part in it.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Abhimanyu fell inside the wheel, and Arjuna made his vow: Jayadratha before sunset, or the fire. Your line: what their promises are worth. Today, the sun is the clock.
screen: `DRONA.` · `A VOW BEFORE SUNSET.`

segments.voice: The news of Arjuna's vow reaches Jayadratha in the night, and he wants to leave the war and go home. Drona talks him out of it. Stay, he says, and I'll protect you. So in the morning Drona builds his army into layer after layer, and places Jayadratha far at the back, behind all of it. Arjuna has one day to cut through to a man hidden behind a whole army. Every hour the sun climbs, then starts to fall.
screen: `JAYADRATHA WANTS TO FLEE.` → `DRONA HIDES HIM AT THE BACK.` → `ONE DAY, ONE SUN.`

segments.voice: Arjuna and Krishna drive into the ranks, and the fighting goes on hour after hour. At one point the horses are worn out. In Ganguli's telling, Arjuna stands guard with his bow while Krishna unyokes them, lets them drink and rest, right there in the middle of the battle, then harnesses them again. It's a strangely tender pause in a day of slaughter. But the sun keeps falling, and Jayadratha is still out of reach. Then the light fails. Darkness spreads over the field, and the text says Krishna brought it about by his own power. The Kaurava side sees what looks like sunset. They cheer. Arjuna has failed his vow. Jayadratha, safe at last, raises his head to look at the sky. Now, Krishna says. The sun is still up. And Arjuna's arrow takes Jayadratha's head. Krishna adds one warning. Jayadratha's father had once declared that whoever made his son's head fall to the ground would have his own head burst. So Arjuna's arrows carry the head away, and it falls into the father's lap as he sits at his evening worship. When the old king rises, startled, the head drops to the earth, and the curse falls on him instead. The epic tells it plainly: Krishna's darkness, a hidden man, a curse turned back on its maker. Some readers find the day troubling. Others see Krishna keeping a vow alive on a field where the rules had already broken around Abhimanyu. And Drona's turn is coming.
screen: `A REST FOR THE HORSES` · `DARKNESS BEFORE SUNSET` · `JAYADRATHA LOOKS UP` · then, large: `THE CURSE TURNS BACK`

segments.voice: Think of something you're racing against today, a deadline, a promise, a clock, and feel on the in-breath how tightly it holds you. On the out-breath, give yourself a pause, the way Krishna gave the horses water in the middle of the fight; the race will still be there. If you pray, let your prayer be the resting place.
Drona. Today he hides Jayadratha behind his whole army, and the hiding place doesn't hold.
screen: `DRONA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the sun is still up. Even a race against the sunset had room to water the horses. Day eight hundred thirty-four, done.

835.title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
835.hook: Karna has one weapon he can use only once, saved for Arjuna, and in the middle of the night he has to decide
835.howItsDone: Ghatotkacha is remembered in Hindu storytelling, and in some regional traditions, as Bhima's loyal son; his night battle and death are told in the Drona Parva of the Mahabharata.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-THIRTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the race against the sun ended with a false sunset and Jayadratha's death. Your line: the sun is still up. Tonight the fighting doesn't stop at dark.
screen: `DRONA.` · `A FALSE SUNSET.`

segments.voice: Lamps. That's what the field looks like now. The armies are so enraged after Jayadratha's death that they keep fighting into the night, and in Ganguli's telling, lamps are lit on chariots and elephants so the warriors can see one another. Darkness belongs to someone on the Pandava side: Ghatotkacha, Bhima's son by Hidimba, a rakshasa, huge and powerful, and strongest at night. He tears into the Kaurava ranks, and they start to break. Today, the weapon Karna has been saving, and who it finally hits.
screen: `LAMPS ON THE FIELD.` → `GHATOTKACHA, BHIMA'S SON.` → `STRONGEST AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Karna carries a dart called the Shakti, a gift from the god Indra. The text tells how he got it: Indra came to him disguised as a brahmana and asked for his natural armor and earrings, and Karna, who would not refuse such a request, cut them from his body and gave them. In return, Indra gave him this weapon, one that would kill any single enemy, but could be used only once. Karna has kept it for Arjuna. Every night he's thought about it. Now the Kauravas are being torn apart by Ghatotkacha, and they beg Karna. Use it, Duryodhana pleads, or none of us will see morning. Karna hesitates, and then he throws. The Shakti strikes Ghatotkacha, and as he falls, the text says, he makes his body enormous, so that even in dying he crushes part of the Kaurava army beneath him. The Pandavas weep for Bhima's son. And Krishna does something that shocks them. He rejoices. He embraces Arjuna. Arjuna asks how he can be glad at a time like this. Krishna explains. The dart that would have killed you is gone now. Karna has spent it. You are safe from it. A son of the Pandava house has given his life, and in doing it he has drawn off the blow meant for his uncle. The epic holds both at once: real grief for Ghatotkacha, and Krishna's relief, and it won't let either cancel the other.
screen: `THE SHAKTI, USED ONCE` · `"USE IT, OR NONE OF US SEE MORNING"` · `GHATOTKACHA FALLS` · then, large: `KRISHNA REJOICES`

segments.voice: Let your hands open on your lap and think of something you've been saving for one particular moment: money, energy, a hard conversation. Breathe in and hold it in mind; breathe out and ask honestly whether you're keeping it for the right moment, or just keeping it, with no need to decide. If you pray, you can name it in your prayer.
Drona. His army fights on into the night, and Karna spends the one weapon he meant for Arjuna.

segments.voice: Your line: has given his life. One dart, kept so long, spent in a single night. See you tomorrow.

836.title: Drona: Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Drona's death
836.hook: Bhima kills an elephant, and then he shouts its name across the field
836.tomorrow: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
836.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's half-truth about Ashvatthama is told in the Drona Parva, and Hindu storytellers and teachers return to it when they talk about truthfulness, dharma and the costs of the war.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Last night Karna spent his one dart on Ghatotkacha, and Krishna rejoiced that Arjuna was safe. Your line: has given his life.
screen: `DRONA.` · `THE DART IS SPENT.`

segments.voice: There's an elephant on the Kaurava side named Ashvatthama. Same name as Drona's beloved son. Bhima finds the elephant, kills it with his mace, and then turns toward Drona and shouts, loud enough for the whole field: Ashvatthama is dead. It's a trick, and it was planned. Drona has been cutting through the Pandava army, and Krishna has told them, in Ganguli's telling, that the teacher can't be beaten while he holds his weapons. But if he hears that his son is dead, he'll put them down. Today, how a truthful man's half-truth ends his teacher's life.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT NAMED ASHVATTHAMA.` → `BHIMA SHOUTS THE NAME.` → `A PLANNED TRICK.`

segments.voice: Drona hears Bhima, and he doesn't believe it. Not from Bhima. There's one man whose word he trusts: Yudhishthira, known for never telling a lie. So Drona asks him directly. Is my son dead? Arjuna won't have any part of the plan. Krishna presses Yudhishthira: there are times, he argues, when a falsehood saves lives. Yudhishthira is afraid of lying, the text says, and he wants victory. So he answers: Ashvatthama is dead. And under his breath, so Drona can't hear, he adds: the elephant. Then the epic adds a detail. Yudhishthira's chariot, the text says, had always moved a little above the earth. After those words, it sinks and runs along the ground like everyone else's. Drona, his heart broken, lays down his weapons. He sits on his chariot and turns inward, in yoga. Dhrishtadyumna, the prince of Panchala, rushes at him with a sword. Arjuna cries out to take him alive. Too late. Dhrishtadyumna strikes, and the teacher of both houses is dead. Here's what the epic won't let go of. The trick worked. The war turned. And the man known for his truth paid for it with the thing he was known for, and the ground itself took note. Drona's command ends here, and Karna will lead next.
screen: `"IS MY SON DEAD?"` · `"...THE ELEPHANT"` · `THE CHARIOT TOUCHES GROUND` · then, large: `DRONA LAYS DOWN HIS WEAPONS`

segments.voice: Think of a time you told a half-truth, the true words with the important part said quietly or not at all, and go gently: no need to punish yourself. Breathe in and remember what you said; breathe out and feel how it sat with you afterward, light or heavy. If you pray, you can bring that moment there.
Drona. The teacher of both houses, who laid down his weapons when the one man he trusted said his son was dead.

837.title: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
837.hook: Karna takes command, and asks for a king to hold his reins
837.tomorrow: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
837.howItsDone: Hindus meet Karna's last battle through recitations and readings of the Mahabharata, retellings, regional theater and television serials; the Karna Parva, the epic's book named for him, tells this part of the war.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Drona, the teacher, fell, and your line was the ground itself took note. Bhishma is down, and now Drona too. So who leads the Kauravas now?
screen: `DRONA.` · `THE TEACHER FALLS.`

segments.voice: A new commander needs a driver. In the Kaurava camp, Duryodhana turns to his friend Karna and gives him the army. Karna accepts, and then he says something honest. Arjuna has an advantage I don't, he tells Duryodhana, in effect: he has Krishna holding his reins. If I'm to face him, I need a charioteer who knows horses the way Krishna does. And Karna names the man: Shalya, king of Madra, the uncle of the Pandava twins, who ended up fighting on the Kaurava side.
screen: `KARNA TAKES COMMAND.` → `ARJUNA HAS KRISHNA.` → `I NEED SHALYA.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana goes to Shalya and asks, and Shalya is furious. In Ganguli's English, the king takes it as an insult: he, a crowned king, told to drive for Karna, who was raised in a charioteer's house. He nearly walks out of the camp. So Duryodhana talks him round. He praises Shalya's skill with horses, calls him Krishna's equal at the reins, and tells an old story of the gods in which the creator Brahma himself drove the chariot for Shiva. Driving, in that story, is no shame. Shalya agrees, with one condition: he'll say whatever he likes to Karna's face. Karna accepts. Now the layer underneath. Before the war began, the epic tells us, Shalya met Yudhishthira and made him a promise. If he ever drove for Karna against Arjuna, he would wear down Karna's courage with his words. So the man stepping into Karna's chariot carries a promise to the other side. Karna asked for a driver to match Krishna, and he got one. He also got a voice in his ear that was never quite his. The story doesn't hurry to tell us how that will go. It just lets the two men climb into the same chariot.
screen: `KARNA ASKS FOR SHALYA` · `A KING TOLD TO DRIVE` · `I WILL SAY WHAT I LIKE` · then, large: `A PROMISE TO THE OTHER SIDE`

838.title: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
838.hook: Shalya keeps his promise with a story about a crow and a swan
838.tomorrow: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
838.howItsDone: Shalya's fable of the crow and the swan is retold in readings of the Karna Parva and in collections of Mahabharata stories, where it can travel on its own as a story about pride.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna took command and asked for Shalya at the reins, a driver with a promise to the other side. Your line was a voice in his ear.
screen: `KARNA.` · `SHALYA AT THE REINS.`

segments.voice: What does a driver say as the chariot rolls out to battle? Karna is in high spirits. Whoever shows me where Arjuna is, he calls across the field, I'll reward him richly. Beside him, holding the reins, Shalya laughs. Save your gifts, he says, in effect. You'll see Arjuna soon enough, and you won't enjoy it. Karna boasts again. Shalya mocks again: two proud men in one small chariot, the army watching. Then Shalya stops arguing and does something sharper. He tells a story.
screen: `KARNA CALLS FOR ARJUNA.` → `SHALYA LAUGHS.` → `A STORY INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's English, it goes like this. A crow lived in a merchant's house, and the merchant's children fed it the leftovers from their plates. Well fed, the crow grew proud. One day some swans came by, and the crow challenged them: I can fly better than any of you. I know more ways to fly than you can name. A swan answered simply: I know one way. They set out over the ocean. The crow showed off, diving and wheeling, every trick it knew. The swan flew straight. Far out over the water the crow grew tired. Its wings dragged, it sank toward the waves with nowhere to land, and it begged the swan for help. The swan lifted the exhausted crow onto its back and carried it back to land. Then Shalya turns to Karna. You, he says, are that crow, fed on the leftovers of Dhritarashtra's sons, and Arjuna is the swan. That's the promise to Yudhishthira, kept: not with an arrow, but with a fable aimed at Karna's courage. Karna doesn't turn back. He answers with hard words of his own, and the chariot rolls on toward Arjuna. And the story inside the story is almost gentle. The swan doesn't gloat. It flies one way, straight, and when the boaster falls, it lifts him up.
screen: `THE CROW FED ON LEFTOVERS` · `I KNOW ONE WAY TO FLY` · `THE SWAN LIFTS THE CROW` · then, large: `YOU ARE THAT CROW`

segments.voice: Let your breath find one simple path: in through the nose, out slowly, no diving and wheeling. Karna. The commander who rides out boasting, and hears his driver tell him he's the crow, and rides on anyway.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shalya told Karna he was the crow and Arjuna the swan, and Karna rode on anyway. Your line was one way, done straight.

segments.voice: Yudhishthira's bow is cut. His chariot is wrecked. He is the eldest of the Pandavas, the man the whole war is being fought to crown, and he stands beaten, within reach of Karna's weapons. One more arrow would do it. And Karna lowers his weapon. He mocks Yudhishthira, tells him to go back to his own kind and leave fighting to warriors, and he lets him go. In the epic he spares Nakula, one of the twins, the same way. Why?
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA IS BEATEN.` → `ONE MORE ARROW.` → `KARNA LETS HIM GO.`

segments.voice: The answer is back before the war, by a riverbank. Karna used to pray facing the sun, and one day, as he finished, a woman was standing in his shadow. It was Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas. She told him what he had never known for certain: she was his mother too. She had borne him as a girl, before her marriage, a son of the sun god, and set him afloat on the river. Now she asked him to come over to his brothers' side. Karna refused. Where were you, he says in effect, when I needed a mother? Duryodhana stood by me when no one else did, and I won't leave him now. But he gave Kunti something. He promised he would not kill her sons, except Arjuna. One of the two of us will die, he told her, and either way you'll keep your sons. So on the field, with Yudhishthira at his mercy, Karna remembers the riverbank. Here's the part that aches. Karna knows, and Kunti knows, and so does Krishna, who had told him of his birth. To Yudhishthira, Karna is the enemy who humiliated him and inexplicably let him live. The brothers don't know they are being spared by their own brother.
screen: `KUNTI AT THE RIVERBANK` · `I WON'T LEAVE DURYODHANA` · `A PROMISE TO HIS MOTHER` · then, large: `THE BROTHERS DON'T KNOW`

Karna. The warrior who could have ended the war with one arrow, and kept a promise to his mother instead, while his brothers never knew why.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna let Yudhishthira go, keeping his promise to Kunti, though the brothers knew nothing about it. Your line was either way you'll keep your sons.
screen: `KARNA.` · `THE BROTHERS DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Wounded and ashamed, Yudhishthira has been carried back to the Pandava camp. Then Arjuna and Krishna ride in from the field, and his face lights up. They've come, he thinks, to tell him Karna is dead. They haven't. Karna is still out there. And the gentle eldest brother, sore from his defeat, turns on Arjuna with words he can't take back. If you can't kill Karna, he says, in effect, give your bow Gandiva to someone who can. Arjuna's hand goes to his sword.
screen: `CARRIED BACK TO CAMP.` → `IS KARNA DEAD?` → `GIVE YOUR BOW AWAY.`

segments.voice: Arjuna, the epic says, had made a secret vow: whoever told him to give his bow to another, he would kill. Now his own brother has said it. Keep the vow, and he kills Yudhishthira. Break it, and he breaks his word. Krishna steps between them and asks a harder question: what is truth, really? He tells two stories. An ascetic named Kaushika had vowed always to speak the truth. Robbers asked him which way some travelers had run to hide, and he told them. The travelers were killed, and the epic says Kaushika suffered for that truthful answer. And a hunter named Balaka killed a creature that was about to destroy all living things, and was honored for it. In Krishna's telling, truth is weighed by what it does to living beings, not only by the letter of a promise. Then he offers a way through. For a man like Yudhishthira, he says, to be spoken to with contempt is a kind of death. So Arjuna speaks harshly to his brother, and keeps his vow without a drop of blood. At once he's sorry. The brothers weep, and Yudhishthira blesses him. Then Arjuna rides out again toward Karna, the quarrel healed. Karna's command began with a bargain over the reins; this week ends with a family pulled back from the edge.
